label: Phishing vs vishing vs smishing vs whaling vs pretexting

mentor.diagnosis: You named the family instead of the specific variant. The exam names the channel and the target.
contrast: Email from a real, compromised account
Defined by the invented backstory, not the channel
mentor.rule: Identify the channel first, then the target. Both are in the stem.
mentor.tell: 'A call from someone claiming to be IT' is vishing. If the message came from the CFO's genuine mailbox, it is business email compromise, not spoofing.
mentor.trap: Phishing is technically true of most of these, so it is always defensible and rarely the most precise answer.

label: Which family a threat vector belongs to: message, file, device, network, software or supply chain

mentor.diagnosis: You classified the vector by the payload or by the eventual damage rather than by the route in. The vector is how the attacker first reaches you, not what happens afterwards.
contrast: Email, SMS, instant message, voice call
A human is addressed directly and asked to act
'received a message', 'a caller claiming to be', a link or a request
A document, executable or image that carries the payload
The content itself is the weapon, however it arrived
'found in the car park', 'handed out at a conference'
open socket in reception, unknown pairing, rogue AP
No one has to be tricked; it is exposed
default credentials, unpatched, vendor ended support, listening port
Trust you granted is used against you
'the MSP agent', 'a vendor update', third-party library
mentor.rule: Ask how the attacker got their first foothold, not what they did with it. A macro-laden spreadsheet sent by email is file-based once you are judging the payload and message-based once you are judging delivery, so the stem will name the one it means.
mentor.tell: Any question listing several plausible ways in and asking which vector or attack surface it is.
mentor.trap: The damage is memorable and the route is not, so people answer with the outcome. Ransomware is not a vector, it is what arrived.

label: Vendor vs supplier vs managed service provider as a threat vector

mentor.diagnosis: You treated every third party as the same vector. The exam separates them by what you handed over: a product, a component, or the keys.
contrast: A finished product or service you bought
Their update or their support access reaches inside
'the vendor's update', 'signed by the maker', 'vendor support portal'
Parts, materials or components that go into what you build or run
A tampered component arrives already inside the product
'a batch of network cards', 'arrived with modified firmware'
Operates something for you, with standing privileged access
Their compromise is your compromise, through credentials you granted
'remote management agent', 'reached dozens of clients at once'
mentor.rule: Vendor sells it, supplier makes the parts of it, MSP runs it for you. The one with standing access is the one whose breach reaches you fastest and widest.
mentor.tell: Any stem where the attacker never touched your network directly and arrived through a trusted third party's product, component or access.
mentor.trap: Vendor and supplier are interchangeable in ordinary speech. The exam uses supplier for upstream components and vendor for the product you bought. And a third party's credentials are not an insider: the person is not your employee.

label: Misinformation vs disinformation, and impersonation vs brand impersonation vs typosquatting

mentor.diagnosis: You named the effect rather than the intent, or the technique rather than the thing being faked. These five are separated by whether the falsehood is deliberate and by what is counterfeited.
contrast: An employee reshares a false outage report they believed
Coordinated accounts invent a product recall
A caller claiming to be the help desk
A login page styled as the bank
examp1e.com, registered to catch mistyped visitors
mentor.rule: Mis- is a mistake, dis- is deliberate. Impersonation fakes a person, brand impersonation fakes an organisation, typosquatting fakes an address.
mentor.tell: 'coordinated', 'campaign', 'fabricated' signal disinformation; 'reshared', 'believed' signal misinformation; a near-miss domain is typosquatting.
mentor.trap: A typosquatted domain usually serves a brand impersonation page, so both are present. The question asks which technique the stem is describing, and a one-character-off address is the typosquatting part.

label: Unsecure wireless vs wired vs Bluetooth, and open ports vs default credentials

mentor.diagnosis: You collapsed every network-side opening into 'the network'. The exam names the specific opening, because each one is closed by a different control.
contrast: A network reachable from outside the walls with weak or no authentication
A live port in a public area
802.1X on the switch port, disabling unused ports, NAC
Non-discoverable mode, pairing confirmation, off when unused
A service anyone can log into with the factory password
Change on commissioning, enforce at provisioning
mentor.rule: Name the opening, then the control that closes exactly that opening. If your answer would also close three other openings, it is the wrong level.
mentor.tell: 'socket in reception', 'unknown device paired', 'factory password', 'listening on port' are each a different vector.
mentor.trap: Default credentials are not a flaw in the software; the software is working as designed. They are a configuration the attacker counts on, and no patch fixes them.
